(עולת תמיד בשם רדב"ז). וצריך עיון דמתחילה שהיו מבדילין בתפילה ודאי היה צריך להבדיל ביום אחד ועכשיו גם כן צריך וכן משמע בגמרא דאם הבדיל על הכוס קודם שהתפלל אף על פי כן צריך להבדיל בתפילה ואין בידי גוף התשובה לעיין בה (מגן אברהם). ויש לומר דשכח להתפלל הוי כמו שהתפלל ושכח להזכיר דאין צריך לחזור ולהתפלל דסמכינן על הכוס וצריך עיון:
eliyah_rabbah.en:
[1] [Levush] Therefore they established, etc. Another reason is that one should not request his personal needs before reciting Havdalah. They therefore established Havdalah in the blessing of knowledge, which is the first of the requests (Abudraham; Rashba, siman 739).
[2] [Levush] And afterward he begins, etc. Malbushei Yom Tov, Piskei Tosafot, Bach, and all the later authorities agree that one should begin Atah Chonantanu before "Grant us knowledge, etc.," and such is the custom. This also appears from the Abudraham cited above, for if one begins it after "Grant us knowledge, etc.," he would be requesting his needs before reciting Havdalah.
[3] [Levush] They are not relevant, etc. See Bach and Lechem Chamudot for explanations of this. One who did not pray on Motzaei Shabbos should pray Shacharit twice the next morning and should not say Atah Chonantanu, even if he did not recite Havdalah (Olat Tamid in the name of Radbaz). This requires study, because originally, when Havdalah was recited in the prayer, he certainly had to recite it the next day, and the same should apply now. The Gemara likewise implies that even if he recited Havdalah over a cup before praying, he must still recite Havdalah in the prayer. I do not have the responsum itself available for examination (Magen Avraham). One may answer that forgetting the entire prayer is comparable to having prayed but forgotten the insertion, in which case he need not repeat the prayer because we rely on Havdalah over the cup. This still requires study.

In Chonen HaDaas, etc., the widespread custom, etc. This excludes the view that one should not say both 'Atah Chonen' and 'Atah Chonantanu,' because that would be repetitive, and that one of them suffices. Even among those who use only one formulation there is a dispute: some say one should begin with the ordinary blessing, 'Atah Chonen l'adam daas,' and then continue into the distinction between sacred and profane, so as not to alter the fixed text established by the Sages. Others say it is preferable to begin only with 'Atah Chonantanu.' The Levush writes to say both, but would say 'v'chonenu me'itcha' twice. The Bach cites and rejects this. Therefore Magen Avraham brings the Bach's formulation: say both 'Atah Chonen' and 'Atah Chonantanu,' but say 'v'chonenu me'itcha' only once at the conclusion. The Bach explains that this is not repetition. First we praise Hashem for granting knowledge to humanity generally, including worldly wisdom, in which Israel and the nations share. Then we praise Him for granting us, Israel, an additional gift: knowledge of His Torah, 'which He did not do for every nation.' Finally we petition, 'Grant us from Yourself,' for both kinds of wisdom, worldly wisdom and Torah wisdom.
And if he forgot, etc. This requires study from the original enactment. Berachos 33a states that when the exiles returned in the days of Ezra they were poor, so Havdalah was instituted in prayer. When they later became wealthy, it was instituted over a cup. When they again became poor, they fixed it in prayer, while also declaring that one who recites Havdalah in prayer must still recite it over a cup.
If so, at the beginning of their return, when Havdalah was instituted only in prayer and not over a cup, one who forgot and neither prayed the proper Amidah nor recited Havdalah would have had to pray Shacharis and include Havdalah in the compensatory prayer, because he had not yet recited Havdalah at all. This is analogous to our law that Havdalah over a cup may still be recited until the end of Tuesday, as explained below in siman 299.
This also appears from the Gemara. There it asks: one who recites Havdalah over a cup, must he also recite it in prayer? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers by an a fortiori argument from prayer: prayer was the primary enactment, yet the Sages said that one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over a cup. All the more so one who recites it over a cup, which was not the primary enactment, should still recite it in prayer.
See Yoreh De'ah, siman 341, regarding an onen on Motzaei Shabbos, who neither prays nor recites Havdalah that night. On Sunday after burial, although he is exempt from a compensatory Maariv, he must nevertheless recite Havdalah over a cup. Siman 299 explains that the time for Havdalah extends through Tuesday.

1) [Seif 1] Havdalah is recited in Chonen HaDaas. This is because one may not request his needs before Havdalah. Magen Avraham, paragraph 1. Another reason is that without understanding, one cannot distinguish. Tosefes Shabbos, paragraph 1.
2) There: In Chonen HaDaas. The custom is to begin, 'You graciously grant knowledge to man and teach understanding to a mortal.' One then recites Atah Chonantanu, and afterward concludes, 'Graciously grant us from Yourself,' etc. Bach. See there for his challenge to Levush. This is also the view of Taz, paragraph 1; Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos Beis Yosef, paragraph 1; Magen Avraham, paragraph 1; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 2; Birkei Yosef in Shiyurei Berachah, paragraph 1.
3) There: If he erred and did not recite Havdalah, etc. If circumstances beyond his control prevented him from praying after Shabbos, he recites two prayers during the day, the first for his present obligation and the second as compensation. He should not recite Atah Chonantanu, although he did not recite Havdalah. Radbaz, volume 1, siman 176, and in the new edition, siman 361; Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos HaTur; Olas Tamid, paragraph 1; Birkei Yosef, paragraph 1. Although Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah question Radbaz's ruling and maintain that he must recite Atah Chonantanu in the compensatory prayer, and Mateh Yehudah, paragraph 2, agrees, nevertheless, since the matter is disputed, passivity is preferable so that he will not interrupt the prayer. According to the opinion that he need not recite it, doing so would constitute an interruption. This applies when he can rectify the omission over a cup, such as when he recited Havdalah over a cup after Shabbos or has a cup over which to recite Havdalah on Sunday. If he has no cup, as in seif 2, however, he must recite Havdalah in the compensatory prayer even according to Radbaz. Mateh Yehudah there. See above, siman 108, paragraph 6.
4) A prayer leader who did not pray after Shabbos should pray Shacharis silently for his Shacharis obligation and recite the second prayer aloud as compensation and to fulfill the obligation of one who is not proficient. Radbaz in the aforementioned responsum. Magen Avraham questions this because of Atah Chonantanu, but Radbaz already explained his words in that responsum; see there. Birkei Yosef, paragraph 2.
5) An onen after Shabbos, who was not obligated to pray, should not recite Atah Chonantanu when he prays Shacharis on Sunday after the burial. Rabbi Moshe Amarillo in Responsa Devar Moshe, volume 3, Yoreh De'ah, siman 15; Birkei Yosef, paragraph 3; Shaarei Teshuvah, paragraph 1.

Maharil implies this even when he has wine for Havdalah. Magen Avraham writes that one should rely on them specifically when he has no cup. Piskei Tosafot, however, writes that even when he has no cup he should not say it in Shomea Tefillah, but must return to Atah Chonen, because only a petition may be inserted in Shomea Tefillah, not a request or mention of another matter, as Beit Yosef writes. Furthermore, Beit Yosef writes that "just as You distinguished us" is itself a prayer. Tanya writes: "He need not say it in Shomea Tefillah because he says it over the cup." This implies that Tanya agrees that when he has no cup, he may say it there.

He should not recite Atah Chonantanu, although he did not recite Havdalah. Radbaz, volume 1, siman 176, and in the new edition, siman 361; Knesses HaGedolah, Hagahos HaTur; Olas Tamid, paragraph 1; Birkei Yosef, paragraph 1. Although Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah question Radbaz's ruling and maintain that he must recite Atah Chonantanu in the compensatory prayer, and Mateh Yehudah, paragraph 2, agrees, nevertheless, since the matter is disputed, passivity is preferable so that he will not interrupt the prayer. According to the opinion that he need not recite it, doing so would constitute an interruption. This applies when he can rectify the omission over a cup, such as when he recited Havdalah over a cup after Shabbos or has a cup over which to recite Havdalah on Sunday. If he has no cup, as in seif 2, however, he must recite Havdalah in the compensatory prayer even according to Radbaz. Mateh Yehudah there. See above, siman 108, paragraph 6.
